AI investment is driving U.S. data center construction at a scale that demands new approaches to financing. J.P. Morgan's Investment Banking teams break down how corporate debt, project-level debt and multi-layered equity structures are being deployed — and what risks developers and investors need to manage. The U.S. data center market is experiencing unprecedented growth, fueled by the rapid adoption of AI, cloud computing and enterprise migration. In 2026 alone, J.P. Morgan estimates capex for the five largest U.S. hyperscalers — large-scale cloud and technology companies — will reach $697 billion, up by $173 billion since the beginning of the year. As John Servidea, global co-head of Investment Grade Finance at J.P. Morgan, said, “AI financing is the biggest secular theme in our professional lifetimes.” The industry ambition is visible in recent transactions. Project Stargate, the AI infrastructure initiative announced by the U.S. government in January 2025, plans to invest up to $500 billion in U.S. data centers and energy infrastructure over four years. J.P. Morgan originated $9.6 billion across two construction loans for the initiative’s Abilene, Texas campus, acting as lead left, sole underwriter and sole structuring agent on both transactions — a single engagement that illustrates the scale of capital now moving into AI infrastructure. “AI financing is the biggest secular theme in our professional lifetimes.” Global co-head of Investment Grade Finance, J.P. Morgan Behind every AI model training run and cloud query sits a physical support structure: purpose-built facilities that require land, power, cooling and connectivity at industrial scale. “That’s digital infrastructure. Most people don’t realize it, but there’s billions of dollars of physical assets supporting virtually every technology experience that you enjoy today,” said Scott Wilcoxen, head of Global Digital Infrastructure Investment Banking at J.P. Morgan. Historically, this infrastructure spanned foundational physical networks including cell towers, fiber-optic cables and satellites. As AI adoption and cloud computing grow, data centers are emerging as the most critical facilities to support increased demand. Not all open land can support industrial-grade utilities and long-term expansion possibilities. Developers must closely evaluate data center build sites based on unique requirements, including: Acreage: According to IBM, the average onsite data center typically has between 2,000 and 5,000 servers, with a footprint reaching 100,000 square feet — roughly the equivalent of 38 standard tennis courts. Connection: The space must offer proximity to power transmission and fiber networks, or the project must consider installation of these connections as part of the build cost. Environmental security: Consideration of earthquakes, floods and other environmental risks is critical to ensure consistent compute capabilities with minimal interruptions. Community considerations: Developers must address concerns from communities near data center build sites prior to breaking ground. This goes beyond paperwork to include public hearings and stakeholder negotiation. Doing so is a crucial step in establishing permitting rights across zoning, building permits, water rights and more. “Data doesn’t move in a vacuum, it moves over a medium.” Head of Global Digital Infrastructure Investment Banking, J.P. Morgan AI infrastructure financing requires both scale and bespoke structuring. The capital needs are large, build timelines are long, and the cash flow profile often differs from what traditional investment-grade markets are accustomed to underwriting. “What’s particularly exciting for us is the level of creativity that is required to finance all of this. Thinking about how to raise this capital in the most efficient way requires a lot of collaboration across teams and markets,” said Servidea. In AI infrastructure, debt most often comes in two core structures: corporate (balance-sheet) debt and project-level debt. Corporate debt allows for speed and flexibility: proceeds can fund capex across data center buildouts, power-related spending, networking and compute without tying the lender to one specific project’s performance. Project-level debt, by contrast, is underwritten primarily to a defined set of project cash flows, often supported by long-term contracts or otherwise high-visibility revenues. The trade-off is less flexibility and more structural complexity, in exchange for tighter lender protections and debt sizing that is anchored to the asset’s own cash generation. The June 2026 financing of Hut 8’s Beacon Point data center in Nueces County, Texas illustrates how project-level debt can be structured around durable, contracted cash flows. J.P. Morgan acted as lead left bookrunner on the $4.25 billion senior secured notes offering, which was 100% pre-leased under a 15-year triple-net lease to a high investment-grade tenant. The transaction achieved a 95% loan-to-cost ratio — the highest ever for a high-performance computing data center bond — and priced at T+165, the tightest spread ever recorded for a data center construction bond. Equity is the risk-absorbing capital in AI infrastructure, used to fund growth and shoulder uncertainties that debt investors typically discount, such as technology obsolescence, ramp-up timing, utilization volatility and customer concentration. In practice, equity is often used to get projects built and scaled, with the expectation that the business can later add more debt once revenues are contracted and performance is more predictable. As capital needs grow, equity financing structures have become increasingly complex, often drawing on multiple layers of the capital stack simultaneously. “More often, forming this capital means going to multiple pockets, across multiple regions and, in many instances, looking across multiple layers of the capital stack and incorporating both structured as well as common equity to ultimately fund these investments,” said Wilcoxen. CoreWeave’s April 2026 capital raise demonstrates how AI-first companies are increasingly drawing on multiple layers of the capital stack simultaneously. J.P. Morgan acted as lead left and active bookrunner on a $5.25 billion combined offering comprising of $1.75 billion in senior unsecured notes and $3.5 billion in convertible senior notes. This deal represents one of the largest combined high-yield and convertible offerings ever executed. It also reflects both the scale of capital required to build and operate AI infrastructure at speed and the sophistication of the financing structures now available across the sector. “Investors are not blindly buying everything. There’s a tremendous amount of capital being deployed, but investors are taking the time to do the credit work, understand the stories and figure out relative value and pricing. To me, that’s a healthy sign for the market.” Global co-head of Investment Grade Finance, J.P. Morgan As the demand for data center capacity grows, pressure builds on key components of the supply chain. According to Wilcoxen, the most crucial of these is power supply. Demand for compute is rising faster than many regional grids can support, and the friction shows up in aging transmission infrastructure, limited local capacity and multiyear wait times to connect to power that can push project timelines out materially. As a result, time to power has become a limiting factor for data center and compute deployments. “Accelerating time to power is a top priority for many of our clients, but the grid infrastructure isn’t there,” said Wilcoxen. “There’s a lot of work to do.” Beyond the grid itself, the supply chain is constrained by natural resources and physical inputs that are harder to scale quickly than capital. Builders must secure available land in the right locations, water access and cooling requirements, and appropriate permitting that determines whether a project can move from plan to energized facility. Clients are responding by securing sites and utility pathways sooner, evaluating alternative cooling approaches where feasible and bringing energy and infrastructure specialists into the diligence process to underwrite power availability and execution risk with the same rigor as the underlying compute demand. Over-building is a parallel risk: AI capital expenditure has, in many cases, outpaced monetization. “The uncertainty around how, when and in what magnitude end-user demand materializes in a monetizable way does make it difficult to plan out over a multiple-year cycle,” said Wilcoxen. As a result, long lead times for power and construction are colliding with rapidly evolving technology cycles and shifting customer needs. In response, many operators and sponsors are trying to structure buildouts in phases, pursue more contracted or pre-committed demand where possible, and maintain optionality so capacity can scale with real adoption. Debt concentration is an emerging systemic consideration as AI’s share of the overall financing market grows rapidly. “I don’t think we’re at a point yet where concentration limits are a huge concern, but it is part of the dialogue because as a portion of the overall market, AI is growing very quickly,” said Servidea. Practically, clients are working to keep funding channels resilient by diversifying capital sources, matching debt structures to cash-flow visibility and avoiding overly correlated exposures to a single counterparty, technology node or demand narrative. The throughline is that the next phase of AI infrastructure buildout will be shaped as much by execution discipline as by the availability of capital. “We’re building the physical underpinnings of the future technological progress of mankind.” Head of Global Digital Infrastructure Investment Banking, J.P. Morgan Investor appetite for AI infrastructure is strong, but it’s not indiscriminate. “Investors are not blindly buying everything. There’s a tremendous amount of capital being deployed, but investors are taking the time to do the credit work, understand the stories and figure out relative value and pricing. To me, that’s a healthy sign for the market,” said Servidea. Rather than jumping on the bandwagon, investors are positioning themselves to finance a long-term buildout, considering downside protection as much as upside. “The red lights would start flashing if it felt like there was blind euphoria. That’s not what we’re seeing,” Servidea said. While AI is a major incremental driver, infrastructure buildout is broader than a single theme. “This entire AI dynamic is additive to an already extraordinarily large investment base,” said Wilcoxen. For instance, public cloud and software-as-a-service (SaaS) models are expected to expand meaningfully in the near future. Compute growth won’t map one-to-one with revenue or usage because efficiencies improve over time, but the direction of travel remains clear: more workloads, more data movement and more always-on digital services will translate into continued expansion of data centers, networks and supporting hardware. The next phase of AI infrastructure will reward platforms that can secure reliable, scalable power, navigate grid access and interconnection timelines, and structure financing around durable demand signals. If AI meaningfully reshapes products and workflows, the practical implication is sustained investment not just in compute, but in the physical and energy foundations that make that compute usable at scale. “When you think about all the different things society will be able to do with AI over the next five years, 10 years, 20 years, it’s really hard to comprehend what that’s going to ultimately require,” said Wilcoxen. “We’re building the physical underpinnings of the future technological progress of mankind.” The data center surge: Building the backbone of the digital age Our experts dive deep into the world of digital infrastructure — exploring the critical role of data centers, fiber, and towers in powering today’s digital economy. They also discuss the risks of overbuilding, and the importance of operational expertise. AI is transforming global economies and revolutionizing industries.  is drawing renewed attention as the largest United States bank folds automation deeper into its operations while a warming capital markets backdrop rekindles dealmaking activity. The story sits at the intersection of two forces reshaping the financial sector this year, and it keeps the lender near the center of market conversation about where big banking heads next. Recent reporting has centered on how the bank is using artificial intelligence to rework parts of its workforce, streamlining tasks that once required large teams. At the same time, capital markets have been thawing after a subdued stretch, lifting underwriting and advisory activity across Wall Street. The combination has placed JPMorgan Chase back in the headlines, with the market watching how efficiency gains and revenue growth interact. Automation at a bank of this scale is less about a single dramatic change and more about many small shifts. Routine document review, client onboarding checks, and back-office reconciliation are increasingly handled by software, freeing staff to focus on complex work. The bank has framed the effort as a way to serve clients faster while managing costs, and the market has been weighing how those savings ripple through the wider expense base. After a quiet period, corporate dealmaking has been picking up. Companies that delayed raising money or pursuing mergers have started to move again, and that revival benefits banks with deep underwriting and advisory desks. JPMorgan Chase, with one of the broadest franchises on the Street, tends to capture a meaningful slice of that activity, so a firmer dealmaking backdrop tends to feed directly into its revenue mix. Beyond the trading floors, the bank's vast consumer arm remains a stabilizing force. Low joblessness has kept most borrowers current on mortgages, auto loans, and card balances, limiting loan losses. Steady household finances give the lender a dependable base of interest-based revenue and fee activity, cushioning the swings that come from more volatile capital markets lines. Size gives a bank like this a distinctive place in the sector. A sprawling deposit base, a national branch network, and leading card and payments businesses mean the company touches nearly every corner of American finance. That breadth lets it absorb pressure in one area while leaning on strength in another, and it explains why moves at JPMorgan Chase are often read as a signal for the broader banking group. Interest rates shape almost everything a bank does. When central bank commentary points toward a steadier, more neutral stance, it eases worries about how much lenders must pay to attract deposits. A calmer rate environment tends to support the spread banks earn between what they pay savers and what they charge borrowers, and that dynamic has been a recurring theme in how the market frames the sector this year. Banking has quietly become a technology contest. The firms that can process transactions cheaply, detect fraud quickly, and personalize digital experiences tend to win share over time. JPMorgan Chase has spent heavily on its technology stack for years, and the current automation push is an extension of that long effort. The market has been watching whether these outlays translate into durable efficiency rather than one-off cost cuts. Large banks operate under close supervision, and rules governing capital cushions, consumer protection, and lending practices are always in motion. A proposal to cap card interest charges has surfaced as one concern that could reshape how card-heavy lenders earn revenue. Changes of this kind rarely land quickly, but the mere discussion tends to move sentiment across the group, and JPMorgan Chase, with its large card book, features prominently in that debate. Bank stocks often serve as a barometer for the wider economy, since lenders sit downstream of nearly every business and household. When the Financial Stocks group performs well within the S&P 500, it frequently signals confidence that credit is flowing and activity is healthy. JPMorgan Chase, as the sector's heavyweight, tends to set the tone, and its results are parsed closely for clues about the state of American commerce. Managing money for affluent households and institutions has become a prized line of work because it produces steadier fee revenue than trading. JPMorgan Chase has expanded its wealth franchise, blending banking, lending, and money management under one roof. That push mirrors a broader industry move toward advice-driven revenue, and it places the firm in direct competition with wealth-focused rivals across the Street. Every lender lives and dies by the quality of its loans. So far, the picture has held up, with delinquencies contained and reserves seen as adequate. Still, the market keeps a careful eye on early signs of strain, particularly in consumer credit and commercial real estate. JPMorgan Chase has generally been viewed as conservatively reserved, which tends to reassure the market during uncertain stretches. Cost discipline has become a defining theme across banking, and automation is the newest chapter. If software can handle a growing share of routine work, banks can serve more customers without expanding headcount at the same pace. The market has been trying to gauge how much of the efficiency gain flows to the bottom line versus how much gets reinvested in technology, hiring in specialized roles, and client-facing tools. Unlike many regional lenders, JPMorgan Chase operates across continents, serving multinational corporations, governments, and institutions. That global reach exposes it to a wider set of economic currents but also spreads its base of activity, so a slowdown in one region can be offset by strength elsewhere. Currency swings, cross-border dealmaking, and international trade flows all feed into how the firm performs. Deposits are the raw material of banking, and a deep, low-cost deposit base is a durable advantage. Households and businesses keep vast sums with the largest banks partly for the sense of safety that scale provides. That stickiness gives JPMorgan Chase a steady funding source, which matters even more when the cost of attracting deposits rises across the industry. Market swings can be a double-edged sword for a bank's trading arm. Periods of turbulence often lift trading revenue as clients reposition, while calmer stretches can dampen activity. JPMorgan Chase runs one of the largest trading operations in the world, spanning rates, currencies, commodities, and equities, so shifts in market volatility feed directly into a meaningful part of its revenue. Even in a digital age, physical branches still matter for relationships and trust. The bank has continued to refine its footprint, closing some locations while opening others in growing markets. The strategy reflects a broader industry balancing act between digital convenience and the human touch that many customers still want when handling major financial decisions. The financial sector remains crowded, with money-center banks, regional lenders, payment networks, and money managers all vying for a share of household and corporate wallets. JPMorgan Chase competes across nearly all of these arenas at once, which is both a strength and a challenge. Its breadth means it rarely dominates any single niche the way a specialist might, yet its diversification helps smooth performance over time. For now, attention centers on how the automation push and the dealmaking revival play out together. The market is looking for signs that efficiency gains are real and lasting, that credit quality stays firm, and that capital markets momentum has staying power. Because JPMorgan Chase sits at the top of the sector, its trajectory tends to shape how the entire banking group is read. The themes shaping JPMorgan Chase today, automation, a firmer capital markets backdrop, steady consumer credit, and a shifting rate environment, extend across the financial sector. Each rival is navigating the same forces in its own way, which is why watchers often treat the largest bank as a lens through which to view the group. The current chapter underscores how technology and market cycles jointly steer one of the economy's most closely followed industries. Deposits form the bedrock of a bank the size of JPMorgan Chase, and the composition of that base matters as much as its sheer scale. Checking and savings balances from tens of millions of households, alongside operating accounts from businesses of every size, give the lender a diversified and durable funding source. Because a large portion of these balances tends to stay put even when conditions shift, the bank enjoys a measure of stability that smaller institutions can struggle to match. The market pays close attention to how deposit balances move, since outflows can raise funding costs while steady inflows reinforce the spread the bank earns. In an environment where savers have grown more attentive to the rates they receive, retaining low-cost balances has become a quiet but meaningful contest across the entire industry. The card business sits at the heart of the bank's relationship with everyday households, blending lending, payments, and rewards into a single product used daily. Card balances generate fee revenue and interest-based revenue while also deepening customer loyalty through points and travel perks. Because cards touch discretionary spending so directly, trends in balances and repayment offer an early read on how confident households feel. When people spend freely and pay on time, the business hums; when they pull back or fall behind, early warning signs appear. JPMorgan Chase has built one of the largest card franchises in the country, which makes it both a beneficiary of healthy consumer activity and a name closely watched whenever questions about household credit surface across the market. Beyond consumers, the bank serves a vast base of mid-sized companies, municipalities, and institutions through its commercial arm. These relationships span lending, treasury services, and advice, tying the bank into the daily operations of businesses across nearly every region and industry. Commercial banking tends to generate steady, relationship-driven revenue that complements the more cyclical swings of trading and dealmaking. It also gives the bank a ground-level view of how the real economy is performing, from manufacturing to services, since the borrowing and cash-management needs of these clients reflect broader conditions. This breadth of commercial relationships is part of what allows JPMorgan Chase to weather softness in any single corner of the economy by leaning on strength elsewhere across its diversified base. Payments processing has quietly become one of the most valuable engines inside a modern bank. Every time a shopper taps a card or a business sends money, a bank with merchant-acquiring capabilities can earn a small slice of the transaction. JPMorgan Chase has poured resources into this plumbing, competing with dedicated payments firms as well as card networks. Because payment volumes tend to grow with commerce and rise as cash gives way to digital methods, this business offers a steady stream of activity tied to the broader shift in how people transact. The scale of the bank's payments operation, spanning consumers, merchants, and large corporations moving money globally, gives it a durable position in a fast-evolving corner of finance where technology and reliability increasingly decide the winners. For a bank that safeguards the savings and data of millions, security is not a side concern but a core function. Protecting accounts against fraud, defending systems from intrusion, and maintaining the trust that underpins every relationship require constant vigilance and heavy spending. JPMorgan Chase devotes substantial resources to defending its digital infrastructure, since a single serious breach could damage the confidence on which the entire franchise rests. As banking shifts further online and automation handles more tasks, the surface that must be defended keeps expanding. This makes security spending a permanent feature of the cost base, and it is one reason large banks with the means to fund deep protection keep an advantage over smaller rivals with thinner resources. A bank of this scale runs on the skill of its people, from branch staff and technologists to traders and advisers. Attracting and keeping talent shapes how well the firm executes, and compensation moves in step with the fortunes of the business. As automation reshapes routine work, the mix of skills the bank needs is shifting toward technology, data, and specialized advice. Managing that transition thoughtfully, retraining where possible and hiring for new capabilities, is a challenge the entire industry shares. The culture that binds such a large organization together also matters, since consistency of service across thousands of locations and countless digital touchpoints depends on shared standards. How the firm navigates this human dimension is a quiet but important part of its story. Because JPMorgan Chase touches so much of American commerce, its own activity doubles as a barometer for the wider economy. Patterns in spending, borrowing, saving, and repayment across its enormous customer base reveal how households and businesses are faring in near real time. When card spending stays brisk and loans perform, it points to steady conditions; when caution creeps in, the bank often sees it early. This vantage point gives the lender a distinctive role in market conversation, since its observations about consumer health and business confidence carry weight. The interplay between these Main Street signals and the bank's own results is part of why the firm is watched so closely as a gauge of the broader financial landscape. AlphaStreet Newsdesk powered by AlphaStreet Intelligence The Chemours Company (NYSE:CC) surged 5.4% on Friday, closing at $15.99, despite three major Wall Street firms slashing their price targets by an average of 33.8%. The specialty chemicals maker drew heavy attention as JP Morgan, BMO Capital, and UBS all issued revised outlooks, yet investors pushed shares higher on trading volume of 285,293. The catalyst came from a trio of analyst moves that painted a decidedly cautious picture. JP Morgan maintained its Neutral rating while cutting its price target from $22 to $15. BMO Capital, keeping an Outperform stance, reduced its target from $26 to $18. UBS also held its Neutral rating but slashed its target from $29 to $18. The average new price target across the three firms now sits at $17, representing modest upside from current levels but a sharp retreat from previous expectations. The counterintuitive rally highlights a disconnect between Wall Street’s revised outlook and market reaction. With a market capitalization of $2.4 billion, Chemours saw shares climb even as analysts collectively lowered their sights by more than a third. The divergence suggests investors may have already priced in the downward revisions, or that the new targets—particularly BMO’s $18 and UBS’s $18—still imply meaningful upside potential from the $15.99 close. The specialty chemicals sector has faced headwinds from cyclical demand patterns and input cost pressures, making analyst recalibrations a recurring theme. Friday’s volume suggests steady institutional interest, though not at levels indicating panic or euphoria. The fact that BMO Capital maintained its Outperform rating despite the target cut indicates at least one firm sees value at current levels, potentially emboldening buyers who view the stock as oversold. title: JPMorgan Resets Knicks Valuation After Lakers Deal - TradingView
content: Madison Square Garden Sports MSGS is getting a powerful new valuation signal after JPMorgan estimated the New York Knicks are worth $11.75 billion, following a record-setting Los Angeles Lakers transaction that reset expectations for marquee NBA franchises. The comparison matters because MSG Sports' entire public-market value is only about $9.8 billion, even though the company owns both the Knicks and NHL's New York Rangers. MSG Sports is a publicly traded professional-sports holding company whose core assets are the Knicks and Rangers, along with development-league teams and a training facility. Its economics are driven by ticket sales, league distributions, sponsorships, suites, merchandise and local media rights. JPMorgan JPM analyst David Karnovsky said, The Lakers are the most relevant comp for the Knicks in our view, given the large DMA [media market], lack of arena ownership, and still significant RSN [regional sports network] fees. He added that the Lakers deal validated the market for marquee NBA franchises. The comparison follows an agreement by Bob Iger and Joshua Kushner to acquire control of the Lakers at a $12.5 billion valuation, about a year after Mark Walter took majority control at a $10 billion valuation. For MSGS investors, the implied discount is difficult to ignore. JPMorgan's $11.75 billion estimate for the Knicks alone exceeds MSG Sports' current market capitalization before assigning meaningful value to the Rangers or other assets. The operating business is also growing. Fiscal fourth-quarter revenue rose 37% to $278.7 million, helped by playoff-related revenue, league distributions, sponsorship and merchandise. The key question is whether private-market franchise valuations can eventually close MSGS' public-market discount. Investors should watch any strategic moves involving team ownership, share structure or asset separation, along with Knicks playoff performance and NBA media-rights economics. The league's new national media agreements are already boosting distributions to MSG Sports. The biggest limitation is that the Knicks are not currently for sale, so an $11.75 billion appraisal does not automatically translate into shareholder value. Still, another premium NBA transaction near or above the Lakers' valuation would strengthen the argument that MSGS shares materially understate the value of the assets they represent. title: Franklin Templeton, JP Morgan AM want tokenized fund KYC on par with stablecoins - ledgerinsights.com
content: A coalition of major asset managers has asked the US Treasury and the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) to modernize know your customer (KYC) rules for tokenized funds. Franklin Templeton, Janus Henderson, JP Morgan Asset Management and WisdomTree want similar treatment to stablecoins, where the GENIUS Act permits KYC to be conducted during on and off boarding but doesn’t require it for each transaction. They have formed the Coalition for Tokenized Markets (CTM). “Registered funds should have the same opportunity to compete on a level playing field. That competition is good for investors and good for U.S. capital markets,” states a July letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and FinCEN Director Andrea Gacki. They have a point. If the equivalent rules were imposed on stablecoins, every user of a stablecoin would have to go through KYC directly with the stablecoin issuer. JPMorgan Chase (JPM) continues to grind higher, ranks first in Investor's Business Daily's Banks-Money Center group and was just added to IBD's Big Cap 20 list. So traders might consider taking some bullish exposure on JPMorgan stock, using options in a limited risk way. One way to do that is by using a bullish butterfly spread. This is a similar idea to the one we looked at Thursday on Valero Energy (VLO). Butterfly spreads involve three different option strikes, all within the same expiration date, and are created using either calls or puts. By trading a butterfly with a bullish bias, we can place the trade cheaply and have a large potential payoff. One way to do this is to set a price target that you think the stock could get to over the next few weeks. Assuming we have a price target of 380 for JPM stock within the next few weeks, let's look at how we can set up a bullish butterfly based on those parameters. First, you buy one Sept. 18 call at 370 a share for $7 apiece. Then you sell two Sept. 18 calls at 380 for $3.50 each. Finally, buy one Sept. 18 call at 390 for $1.50. This trade only costs around $150 per spread on a 100-share contract, but has a payoff potential much higher than that. The ideal scenario is for JPM to be right around 380 at expiration on Sept. 18. The maximum loss on the trade is equal to the premium paid of around $150 per contract. This would occur anywhere below 370 or above 390. The maximum potential profit on the trade is $850. Calculate this by taking the width of the butterfly, or $10, multiplied by 100. Then subtract the $150 premium paid. Taking a low-risk trade like this can be one way to gain exposure to a bounce in JPMorgan Chase without risking too much capital. Also, JPMorgan has already reported second-quarter earnings, so this trade should have no earnings risk if held to expiration.
